title: Character Select
subtitle: Thoughts about fiction, and reviews of Stendhal, Nabokov, and others
contentHtml:
(I’ve been cleared to travel again in a month, so this newsletter will soon return to regularly scheduled programming. In November I’ll be in Minneapolis, then Sioux Falls, SD — for a Midwest studies conference — followed by Seoul, Shenyang, and Okinawa. Assuming no additional health issues.)

I read novels for entertainment, but also to learn about culture because they reflect the societies that produce them, offering an ethnographic portrait of a place and time that can be hard to access by other means, especially in the distant past.

I’m particularly interested in the archetypes they reveal — the array of roles a society makes available, the models of personhood we can inhabit. Think of character selection in a video game.

These characters change from place to place and through time — novels both portray them and can change them. National stereotypes are no longer in vogue (deservedly so when they’re used to judge individuals), but they are largely correct. They are folk ethnography, a shorthand summary of the most popular choices on a culture’s character-select screen. The Japanese salaryman, the entrepreneurial American, and the English pub-dwellers are caricatures, but they are caricatures of the most popular roles available.

I’ve written several times before about my belief that every culture does this, because it’s one of the most consequential ways thick culture1 shapes life. Humans are cultural creatures, imbued with the ability to live any type of life, but only choosing to live one. Unlike any other animal, we hold the potential for many different selves, yet we settle into just one, and that self is a manifestation of where and when we grow up.

A rat in Vietnam is almost no different from a rat in Chicago. Its ratness is determined from birth, and its ratness survives moves in time and space. Humans are very different. While we share a common humanness, it’s buried deep enough that we identify far more strongly as Javanese, South Side Chicagoan, or observant Muslim Jordanian. As Wittgenstein wrote decades ago, “If some people looked like elephants and others like cats, or fish, one wouldn’t expect them to understand each other and things would look much more like what they really are.” That is, culture imbues us with such different ways of living, thinking, and comprehending, that we might as well be different species. We are culturally groomed, from birth — molded by the local community’s conception of what a human is, no matter what character we choose to be2.

That might sound harsh, and confrontational, especially in our modern world steeped in a kumbaya campfire secular humanism so intent on highlighting our similarities, a soft cuddly notion that trickled down into popular culture as ads claiming our differences can be overcome by simply sharing a Coke, that it sees the differences as only skin deep.

Yet, there are plenty of differences beyond appearance, embedded into the core of who we are, and how we see ourselves — our work ethic, concepts of honor, relationship to authority, attitude toward family obligations, definition of a successful life, conception of good and evil, and our understanding of beauty, art, and leisure.

For several decades it became intellectually fashionable to try and find human cultural universals, but in the end anthropologists found none. Or none that weren’t, as Clifford Geertz noted, either too trivial (we all need food) or too abstract (we all have a sense of justice) to divine much of anything about the human condition.

That doesn’t mean any group is not human, or without a soul (I am a Catholic who believes in universal human dignity after all), but that becoming one big happy global family isn’t an easy task, certainly not one that’s a shared Coke away.

Any traveler knows this, especially modern travelers, because while globalization has rendered our physical landscapes similar, you still feel like a stranger in a strange land. When in a foreign culture you are still an alien, and with that comes all sorts of misunderstandings, confusions, and imbalances3.

While this is a largely deterministic way to see human behavior — that we are products of our culture, formed without choice — I’m not dogmatic here. Individuals can forge their own path, but even then they are overcoming outside forces, some they recognize, some they don’t. Through life everyone encounters good and bad roles, and which one you move towards, a choice, is what we call personal responsibility. Think of it as the decision points in a game — do you go through door A or B? There are thousands of them, even after you have done a character select, and while some are done without full understanding of the consequences, because culture is so ingrained it’s often not obvious, others are clearly delineated. As a Catholic friend of mine noted, “You will encounter decency in your lifetime — move toward that. That’s a personal responsibility.”

Because people are a product of their environment, in the broadest sense of that word, having a positive culture is essential — it’s far harder to emerge from a corrosive culture a good person than from a functional one. Growing up in a dysfunctional culture is akin to having to run a gauntlet of challenges, and while many can pass all the tests, more will fail than succeed.

In that sense I side with what is now considered the left in suggesting “bad people” are to be treated with more forgiveness, or at least understanding, when they come from difficult circumstances, but I side with the right in that the solution is to focus on changing the culture, rather than absolving all of their mistakes.

Changing culture is far harder though, because it’s not only about policy but about values and those are nebulous and yet have inertia, like a physically impossible heavy gas — push on it, if you can find it, and it settles back exactly where it was.

If a child grows up surrounded by cruelty, disorder, nihilism, crudity, avarice, instant gratification, without beauty or the celebration of the Good, then they are going to be more drawn to disorder, and the negative archetypes it offers.

So what does any of this have to do with novels? Because novels can be guide books to the archetypes of a culture, and they can also change them.

Don Quixote is an obvious example — the title character is a corrupted product of the then ubiquitous chivalric romances that elevated, celebrated, and romanticized a concept of masculine heroism. Through satire, Cervantes is also attempting to change that outdated archetype, to say, “we need new characters.” I doubt he could have predicted that within a hundred years, quixotic would become a word to describe the deluded romanticist, but I’m guessing he would have been happy he’d “reformed” society.

That is one of the salient distinctions between high literature and low, with low being stocked with pure archetypes, cartoonishly so and consequently unrealistic and unachievable. Its aim is to entertain, and in the process it perpetuates those archetypes in a society. High literature has more nuanced portrayals, and its aim is often to reform society. It is elites doing what elites do, which is to change the thick culture.

Notable exceptions are the Odyssey and Iliad, works which are now viewed as high art, but I’d argue they were initially not that. They were immensely popular works — with the original so compelling that fans demanded a sequel. They were akin to our big-budget Hollywood hits, that everyone had to see, and everyone knew everything about, and spent hours debating plot points, character flaws, etc. They even spawned a famous work of fan fiction, with the Aeneid.

That’s why you should read them, because given how much they dominated ancient western culture, they are effectively its user manuals on how to be a person. The heroic man, as rendered by Homer, loomed large over Greek and Roman culture, to the point ambitious men measured themselves against the characters. Alexander the Great, as he marauded across the world, trying to conquer it, carried a copy of the Iliad, supposedly putting it under his pillow each night, and Caesar famously compared himself to Alexander.

Literature after Don Quixote is more self-aware, more inward-looking, more calculated — but equally valuable as a culture guide, not unlike an anthropologist’s field notes. You just have to take the writer’s bias into consideration.

I write all this because for the last month of being medically grounded I’ve spent my time walking, listening to audiobooks, and reading physical books, and below are capsule reviews of several of them. Not all are about archetypes, but all of them made me think about how culture works, and about literature’s role in that, and how we view ourselves.

At a minimum, every novel is a product of the times, even science fiction, which tells us more about the fears and concerns of when it was written than the future. (Pick up any Sci Fi book and within a few pages you can tell when it was written.)

So, in no particular order, here are some novels I’ve been reading. I’m always looking for new suggestions!

The Red and the Black (Stendhal)

(Obviously that photo is not of The Red and the Black, which I read while in Australia, and then gave away to another reader. I’ve only just started The Charterhouse.)

The Red and the Black is a fantastic book, and now is in my top ten novels of all time. It is the book that started me thinking about novels and archetypes because that’s explicitly what it’s about — in this case how in 1830 France for an ambitious man without connections the two roles available were the military (red) and the clergy (black) — two very different understandings of the heroic.

It might be the most “based” classic I’ve read. The main character, Julien, tries both the red and black but is unwilling to accept either of them because he’s fixated on a prior, and unrealistic, heroic role — that of Napoleon. Frustrated there is no place for him, unable to control his desires, so intent on his greatness, he is willing to break everything, and anyone. A man fighting against a culture that he doesn’t believe respects his genius. It is a remarkably modern portrait of hubris, and how a dysfunctional culture both creates that, and channels it into tragedy.

The main character, presumably like other testosterone-driven glory-seeking young men of the era, wants, like his role model, to make an impact on the world and be celebrated, and that desire for greatness is his modus operandi. It is the motor that drives the plot, taking him through all of French society. In that way it’s a road movie, but through culture, not geography.

At times it reads like a soap opera, in the best possible way (entertaining), with every cheap plot device dragged out to shock, illustrate a hypocrisy, while also moving the show along to next week’s installment.

Roberto Bolaño, one of my favorite authors, said all his novels were detective stories, and after reading that quote I realized he was right — not in a hit you over the head way, but at the core of each of his works is a mystery to be solved. I believe all my favorite novels are either detective stories, road trips —again, not pedantically, but as a manic journey through land or society — or both. The Red and the Black is a road trip, that turns into a detective story, although with the mystery revealed and the courtroom the setting.

It joins my other favorite novels, all of which are a mixture of road-trip and mystery. 2666 is explicitly a detective story, layered on additional detective stories, bringing the reader through countries, cultures, and time. Moby-Dick is both a journey and a quixotic quest, Brideshead Revisited a slow mystery about faith, doubt, and uncertainty, and Out, a thriller set in marginalized Japan. Great Expectations might be the exemplar of this mixed genre, with a central mystery propelling Pip through the most substantial geography of 19th-century England — class.

PS: So far The Charterhouse is as good, and covers similar ground, with the famous Waterloo section a deliberate deconstruction of military romanticism.

Lolita (Nabokov)

Phenomenal, now in my top ten novels. Poetic, impish, and perhaps the single best description of driving across the US. If you think there is anything erotic or prurient about Lolita you’re missing the point — it’s about how relationships built around titillation rather than genuine connection become instruments of enslavement, turning another person into an object of one’s own desires.

As Nabokov said in an interview (with Playboy!), “Sex as an institution, sex as a general notion, sex as a problem, sex as a platitude—all this is something I find too tedious for words. Let us skip sex.”

There is also a lesson in rhetoric here, with Nabokov showing how the erudite, with beautiful words, and enough historical and literary references, can justify anything, to themselves and, they hope, others. In that way, it’s a criticism of the old world he himself (and the narrator HH) came from.

That beautiful rhetoric silences Dolores herself, and if there is a moment of revelation it comes near the end (spoiler alert!), when Humbert is standing, broken, bloody, and beaten, in a cow pasture, and remembers sitting on a rock overlooking a small town (described so poetically, because he focuses on everything except his crime) and finally hearing children’s voices, with the lesson being the childhood he eliminated. But this is Nabokov and he respects the reader enough he doesn’t write that point in big bold letters on the chalkboard. Life isn’t neat platitudes, it’s complex enough that only an overly educated intellectual, especially one with an alliterating pseudonym, could possibly think he’s figured it all out.

It’s a monstrously funny book, despite the material, which I presume is supposed to make you uncomfortable, which it did for me, and there were times it was too much and I quit, but I kept picking it back up again because of how well written it is, and the scenes from the road. Nabokov spent summers crossing the country with his wife, staying in small hotels, to collect butterflies, his passion outside of writing, and that clearly is what he is drawing on. He is in love with the landscape of America, but not the culture, the kitsch, vulgarity, and philistinism. It is an ethnography of postwar US, with Nabokov both the outsider observing America and an artist delighted by its physical variety. Two images, out of hundreds and hundreds, stuck with me:

“Or again, it might be a stern El Greco horizon, pregnant with inky rain, and a passing glimpse of some mummy-necked farmer, and all around alternating strips of quick-silverish water and harsh green corn, the whole arrangement opening like a fan, somewhere in Kansas.”

“At night, tall trucks studded with colored lights, like dreadful giant Christmas trees, loomed in the darkness and thundered by the belated little sedan.”

It’s also explicitly a road-trip novel, as well as at times a mystery, although it’s rich enough to fit into many different boxes, without ever being confined to one.

As to archetypes, HH blames his obsession on a lost childhood love, Annabel, while mocking anyone who would reduce his “justified” desire to quack psychology. Nabokov despised Freud, and isn’t offering that as an explanation for his depravity, but as one more excuse. Self-serving determinism wrapped in beautiful prose.

It’s a reminder that while our upbringing shapes us, we are still responsible for which door we walk through.

Last point. Novels can change culture, and writers (or any artist) putting out smut, or crass degrading works, make things worse. While I’m not for censorship, all artists have a responsibility for their choices. Lolita was controversial when written, and still is, yet while it can be exceedingly uncomfortable to read, it’s also a conservative work (in the philosophical sense). If there’s an implicit moral, it’s that the true coarseness is treating another person as an object of your own selfish gratification, however clever your case for justifying it, whether beautiful prose or Freud. That’s an argument against smut.

Tortilla Flat (Steinbeck)

If I can’t have a detective story, or a road trip, then I at least need humor and Tortilla Flat is hilarious, in a comedy of manors (or manners) way, although comedy of flop-house is more appropriate. It’s about a group of winos in the hills above Monterey, CA, Steinbeck’s writing home, and their quest to do nothing, until that’s disrupted by winning the lottery by inheritance of homes, which upends their nothingness, threatening to make respectable characters of them, which they won’t have.

It’s Steinbeck’s first successful novel and it’s his most philosophically conservative, because while empathetic, poverty here is a choice, not a condition imposed by forces beyond the poor’s control.

That said, he’s not a scold, or even a moralizer, and the chaotic self-destruction of dysfunction isn’t reduced to the clinical. He loves the winos because they know themselves, and are true to who they are. Within the nothingness is a society, complete with status hierarchies, roles to inhabit, and a wealth of unwritten rules on behavior. You can cheat, steal, and philander — but if you cheat, steal, and philander in the wrong way, then you’re ejected, forced to serve time making amends, or paying a fine in gallon jugs of homemade wine.

You can see Steinbeck’s liberalism lurking in those details — no group, no minority, not even drunk hobos, is without sophistication. You have to look harder to see it, but it is there.

Almost all current novels about poverty are either a maudlin preachy paternalism — with the poor infused with perfect nobility — or a nasty condemnation with the poor subhuman, and this is neither, and that’s refreshing.

What about archetypes? Steinbeck plays with that idea, even invoking the legacy Don Quixote mocked, with Danny’s house as the Round Table and his friends as knights. They are living out a chivalric archetype, but in a flophouse.

A comic code of honor among winos, with Steinbeck as the ethnographer, not the moralizer.

While I don’t think he entirely pulls off the Round Table analogy — it feels forced at times — his point is correct and something I’ve seen myself. Even in chaos, social norms — including honor, decency, and sin — flourish.

I might be a thieving wino, but I’m not an animal.

East of Eden (Steinbeck)

Excited by Tortilla Flat I moved to Steinbeck’s favorite of his novels, and after a hundred pages I gave up. While the bones of Tortilla Flat are there — exceptional prose, engaging story, a sense of place — the humor is gone, the void filled with dry sermons. While I appreciated the drive through 1880s America it was just too heavy handed for me, with a contrived plot, over the top characters, and a sanctimonious style. It reads like a twenty-five hour self-indulgent morality play and I wasn’t in the mood for that.

This Steinbeck doesn’t trust or respect his readers, and he’s moved from observer to educator, and not a very smart one at that. He begins some chapters with what he clearly believes are his earth-shattering insights into man’s condition, and none of them are notable, beyond their mediocrity and pomposity. They have all the depth of a freshman dorm late night conversation, but without the intoxicated giggles.

For me, juxtaposed next to Tortilla Flat, the lesson is that for fiction to work as ethnography, if it is going to preach rather than observe, the lessons need to be woven into the characters’ actions. Or, if the author is going to moralize directly to the reader, then at least make it entertaining and insightful.

Charles Dickens, one of my all-time favorite authors, is also prone to moralizing, overdrawn characters, contrived plots, but he’s a joy to read because there’s always humor lurking beneath.

With East of Eden I didn’t chuckle once. Didn’t crack a smile.

Tana French Novels

Tana French is one of the best current writers, and because she literally writes detective novels that are exceedingly popular, she’s often overlooked as serious. Which is unfortunate because her work is serious. It is complex, engaging, and well written, with characters with the nuances of genuine people. She understands all classes of society, and her novels have a sense of place that is thoughtful and immersive. You know she knows what she is writing about, which is downscale Ireland.

I used a picture from my walk, rather than a physical book, because I listen to her novels, which especially fits, because she’s a former actress, and they read like narrated theater, with emphasis on dialogue and stage setting. Accents (and hence class) matter, and a good narrator brings that out.

They are whodunits, and while the mystery can draw you in4, that is almost ancillary to the motivations of the characters.

She has ten novels, broken into two series and a standalone, but you needn’t read them in order. The only one I think is a bit of a miss is the first, In the Woods, and for me that was largely due to a bad narrator (in the US audiobook).

My standouts are Broken Harbor, which is one of the best books about the 2008 financial crisis, or at least how it impacted most people, The Trespasser, which is about loyalty and how people inhabit archetypes, and The Witch Elm, a quiet slow meditation on memory, family, and how we see ourselves.

She reminds me of John le Carré, another writer I admire, in that she gets pigeonholed as “just a genre writer” when she is so much more than that.

1

When I write culture here I’m primarily referring to thick culture, what de Tocqueville called mores — “the different concepts men adopt, the various opinions that prevail among them and to the whole collection of ideas that shape mental habits” — rather than thin, which is the more obvious surface level differences such as cuisine, dress, music, etc.

2

Every one of us grows up as part of a community. As Aristotle said, “He who is unable to live in society, or who has no need… must be either a beast or a god.”

3

Run a thought experiment. Imagine being in Tokyo, or Uganda, or even in another neighborhood in your own city that’s of a different class, and make everyone look the same. All our obvious ethnic physical differences are erased. I can guarantee that after half an hour you will still know you are an outsider in a foreign land.

4

I’ve found myself walking an additional five miles, simply to keep the book going. As much as I love my daily walks, there are times I need the additional entertainment!
